paper_title: REA: A Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Foundation models are becoming remarkably reliable at high-level reasoning, yet they remain too slow and costly to serve as fine-grained controllers. Conversely, fast policies like VLAs and whole-body controllers offer more efficient reflexes, but struggle to generalize. While pairing a deliberative brain (foundation models) with a reactive cerebellum (fast policies) seems natural for embodied systems, two obstacles remain: methods are built and scored on incompatible stacks, and their asynchronous coordination is difficult. For example, an agent that calls the VLA in the agentic loop can stall the fast execution, while a VLA that calls the agent on errors tends to re-trigger fallbacks repeatedly or completely miss silent failures. To address this, we propose REA (Routed Embodied Agent), a unified runtime where a deliberative System 2, an embodied router System 1 and reactive System 0 policies cooperate under a single golden rule - no running policy waits on the brain. Instead of querying the brain at each failure, REA employs a route memory that stores each policy's measured success ahead of time, a boundary-triggered judge gate that consults the brain on policy execution, and a shared-budget escalation ladder for bounded recovery. Evaluated on 3,000 test episodes across 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success and beats the best single-agent baseline in its own policy pool (94.7%) while reducing control steps by 25% and control time by 17%. In a separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study, REA achieves 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for the strongest single VLA baseline MEDex. These results demonstrate learned and programmatic policies operating within the same runtime. REA also transfers to BEHAVIOR-1K and a real Unitree G1 humanoid, achieving the highest observed success among the compared methods.

Introduction Foundation-model agents have become capable embodied brains: coding agent can write manipulation program that calls segmentation, grasp planning and inverse kinematics [1, 2], and language or visionlanguage model can decompose command [35] or tell whether task succeeded [5, 6]. These abilities are expensive: in our runs ASPIREs repair loop [2] spent median of 43 min per LIBERO task, and Codex + GPT-6 pipeline consumed 89M input tokens to generate programs for 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks. Nor can the brain simply act as the controller: in our probes, models emitting one-token or Cartesian IK actions solved 1 of 1,987 and 0 of 600 LIBERO-Pro episodes (Appendix C.4, Figure 6). Visionlanguageaction models (VLAs) [710] and whole-body controllers such as SONIC [11] act at few to tens of hertz, far faster than an agent deliberates, but VLAs that exceed 90% on LIBERO collapse under LIBERO-Pros perturbed test set [12]. Embodied intelligence should therefore separate deliberative brain from reactive cerebellum, as recent dual-system robot models do [1317]. However, two obstacles still stand in the way. First, there is no common runtime for comparing agents and VLAs: agentand VLA-based systems are each built on their own simulator, robot, observation format and success criterion, so it is hard for them to test on the same episodes. Second, asynchronous coordination is hard (Figure 3). When the agent drives and calls the fast policy, the fast loop waits on every agent decision: an agent advisor that the router waits for leaves the robot idle for 2.6s per LIBERO-Pro episode, 20% of its control time (Figure 4). When the fast policy drives and calls the agent on errors, persistent error re-triggers the brain at every recurrence, while most failures raise no error at all: an exception-triggered router escalated only 6 times in 590 LIBERO-Pro episodes although 166 failed. Re-execution is not always reliable either: if the task has already succeeded, running it again may undo the result. We address the above issues with REA, Routed Embodied Agent runtime (Figure 1) designed to unify agent and VLA runtime across simulators and real robots. REA implements three-level system: System 2, the brain, is an agent that generates policies offline or online, and provides advises or judges; System 1, the embodied router, decides which policy to run and when to consult the brain without blocking running policy; System 0, the cerebellum, holds fast policies (frozen programs, VLA policies or whole-body controllers) that return control to the router at segment or policy boundaries. REA also provides unified evaluation framework for any policies including code-as-policies and VLAs. Figure 2 shows REA across simulators and on real robot. Our central idea is to let the brain prepare policies offline and intervene online only when there is need, so that no running policy has to wait for it. Besides the conventional serial execution mode, our REA also offers asynchronous mode: policies run at their own rate, with System 2 running in parallel to provide advice or judge. Our proposed method achieves this via three designs. To keep the brain off the dispatch path, REA contains route memory of each policys per-task success and cost on development episodes, so choosing policy can be isolated from the System 2s reasoning process and call System 2 on dilemma. To catch silent failures without re-firing on errors, boundary-triggered judge gate consults System 2 concurrently and decides whether task is finished: if not done then escalates, if done then stops and protects completed work. To keep recovery bounded, an escalation ladder dispatches the next policy from the current state under one shared step and time budget. Results. Routing efficiency. On 3,000 test episodes across all 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks, REA reaches 95.9% success, exceeding the strongest individual baseline, Agents SDK + GPT-6 (94.7%; 𝑝=0.004), and coming within 1% of hindsight per-task oracle. It is the fastest timed method, with 17% less control time than Agents SDK + GPT-6 and 25% less than blocking advisor. Failure recovery. REA improves ASPIRE and zero-shot GPT-6 policies by +8.6% and +7.0%. Contributions. (1) REA, three-level runtime with common contract for agents, VLAs and programmatic policies, evaluated across three simulators and real robots. (2) An embodied router combining route memory, boundary-triggered judge gate and shared-budget escalation ladder to coordinate slow brains and fast policies without blocking execution. (3) Over 30,000 aligned test episodes verifying the contributions of routing and judging, plus separate RoboTwin 2.0 study comparing VLA policies and mixed VLAcode pool within the same runtime. 2. Related Work Embodied brains and fast policies. Large models serve as the deliberative layer of robot systems: SayCan [3] grounds LLM plans in learned affordances, PaLM-E [5] embeds observations into language model, and Inner Monologue [4] and SayPlan [18] re-plan from feedback. Code-as-policy methods let the agent write the controller: Code as Policies [1] and ProgPrompt [19] compose perception and motion primitives, Voyager [20] iterates on executable policy code with environment feedback (Eureka [21] does so for reward code), and ASPIRE [2] scales repair and evolutionary search to LIBERO; more generally, ReAct [22] interleaves reasoning with actions and Reflexion [23] adds self-reflection across trials. At the other end, visionlanguageaction models such as RT-2 [7], OpenVLA [8], Octo [9] and 𝜋0 [10] act far faster than an agent deliberates but generalise within their training distribution [12], and whole-body controllers such as SONIC [11] track motions commanded from above. REA keeps the agent as System 2, off the control loop and the dispatch path, and lets any fast policy serve as System 0. Dual-system control. Following Kahneman [24], GR00T N1 [13] and Helix [14] train slow VLM with fast action head that run at fixed, different rates, and Helix 02 [15] adds learned 1 kHz whole-body System 0; Hi Robot [16] and Gemini Robotics 1.5 [17] let VLM planner command VLA, and real-time chunking [25] overlaps VLAs inference with its execution. Every level there is learned model of one stack. REA keeps the level names but not their semantics: System 1 is router that emits no actions, any policy can serve as System 0, and System 2 is an independently developed agent that no running policy waits for. 4 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control Figure 3 Three ways to couple slow brain with fast policies. (a) An agent that calls the fast policy puts its latency on every step. (b) fast policy that calls the agent on errors is interrupted by persistent errors and never by silent failures. (c) REA dispatches from route memory, lets each policy run uninterrupted at native rate, and consults the System 2 judge only when there is need. Routing, evaluation and completion judging. FrugalGPT [26] cascades LLM APIs, Lu et al. [27] learn reward-guided routers, mixture-of-experts layers [28] gate per token, and Agent-as-a-Router [29] routes each coding task using the verified outcomes of similar past tasks; REAs route memory brings outcome-based routing to embodied policies. Embodied Agent Interface [30] and SIMPLER [31] each evaluate one family of methods, LLM planners or VLAs, whereas REA runs brains, routers and policies of different families on identical episodes. VLMs serve as success detectors [6] and reward models [32], LLM judges score model outputs [33], and REFLECT [34] turns detected failures into corrections; REA proposes no new detector, only where one sits: once per policy return, gating escalation under shared budget and never used as the success criterion. 3. The REA Runtime REA answers one question: how can slow, general brain and fast, narrow policies cooperate without the brain ever blocking running policy? REA variants. REA denotes the shared runtime. Its three variants in experiments differ in policy selection and recovery, see details in Algorithm 1 and Appendix B.1: REA-M (route memory). Uses route memory to select policies and the exception gate to trigger recovery after an exception or truncation, with no online System 2 calls. REA-A (agent routing). Calls System 2 agent to select the initial policy and choose recovery policy whenever the exception gate triggers. REA-V (visual judging). Uses route memory to select policies and visual judge at policy returns to decide whether to stop (done) or advance along the escalation ladder (not_done). 5 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control Figure 4 Task success and control time on LIBERO-Pro. Without route memory the judge ladder is Fix, Evo, Fix; blind retry re-runs Fix once. 4.2. Routing Beats Each Policy-Generation Baseline Routing, not larger pool, makes the gain. Table 1 compares REA with each source method evaluated alone on the same episodes. Choosing one method globally on development data selects Agents SDK (94.7%); choosing method per task at random gives 78.2%. Route memory chooses per task on the same development seeds and reaches 95.9%, +1.2% over the best method (86:51, 𝑝=0.004, paired 95% CI [+0.4, +1.9]%). The comparison is exact on the 37 aligned tasks, where the pool holds only the programs used by the individual baselines: there REA-M reaches 95.3% against 93.7% (54:25, 𝑝=0.001, CI [+0.6, +2.5]%), within 1.0% of the hindsight oracle over the whole pool; on the other 23 tasks it is on par with the best method (96.8 vs. 96.3%). It also costs less: 1,003 steps per success versus 1,343 (25%), because each task goes to its most reliable policy on development episodes (the SDK program on only 14 of the 60 tasks), and those policies are shorter. Per program, routing uses less data than policy generation. Route memory uses 10 development seeds per program (1,790 episodes) and no model tokens, whereas each generation pipeline spent 1,2491,328 development episodes and 2989M input tokens on its own library (Appendix A.2). Route memory is as good as an agent at dispatch: REA-A reaches the same 95.9% (26:26 paired) and, as Section 4.3 shows, is slower. Putting the brain in the control loop does not substitute for policies. Show-Harness, which asks gpt-6-astra for every move from the images, solves 78 of the 3,000 episodes (2.6%); 2,806 of them end at the 900 budget, after 34 model calls on average. 4.3. Route Memory Reduces Waiting for the Agent Figure 4 measures the designs of Figure 3 on one host and one policy library (numbers in Table 4). Waiting for the brain is expensive. An agent advisor that the router waits for, although consulted only 1.7 times per episode, leaves the control path idle 2.62 per episode (20% of its control time), delays the first action by 1.5 s, and is slower than one SDK program (13.33 vs. 12.04 s) with no gain in success. Its advice also costs success, nearly all at the first dispatch: it overrides the policy selected by route memory in 1,236 episodes, on which that policy alone solves 1,168 and the advisor 1,124 (rest: 1,708 vs. 1,699). Route memory removes the wait at its source. REA-M has the lowest control time among the timed methods and ties REA-A for the highest success: 3.37 (25%, CI [31, 20]%) with +1.8% of success against the blocking advisor (90:37, 𝑝<105), and 2.08 9 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control Figure 6 Where should System 2 sit? LIBERO-Pro seeds 110 (600 episodes per method). Left: success with Wilson 95% intervals; the two direct policies solve no episode (arrows at the axis edge). Right: seconds per episode spent in System 2 calls (agent, caption model or text judge), log scale. The direct policies act through 3 cm / 15 Cartesian IK steps and gripper command, at most 80 decisions, from scene captions. Calls and paired counts in Table 5. (17%, CI [23, 11]%) against Agents SDK + GPT-6 in its own campaign. The first gap is not hardware: both methods execute control step in 10.310.4 ms outside System 2 waits. REA-A, whose agent reads the same route memory, matches its success but is 1.39 slower per paired episode: 0.73 waiting for its selection call, the rest because it starts different program in 46% of episodes. 4.4. REA Improves Policies from Different Methods On ASPIREs Fix-loop policies (LIBERO-Pro seeds 110, 590 episodes; Table 7), REA-M alone lifts success from 66.3% to 71.9% (+5.6%, 49:16, 𝑝<104) while reducing steps per success (1,467 vs. 1,557): it escalated on an exception only 6 times although 166 episodes failed, so nearly all of the gain is route memory running the Evo policy first where development favoured it. The judge gate (REA-V) adds further +3.1% (37:19, 𝑝=0.022), for 74.9% in total, at 2.1 the wall time per success (Figure 10). This paired contrast is the gates net effect; how it splits into rescued failures, undone successes and replay variance is only approximate, because REA-Ms own run stands in for REA-Vs first run  (Table 14)  . On zero-shot GPT-6 policies, threefold weaker library, REA-V lifts success from 19.3% to 26.3% (50:8, 𝑝<104); the comparison is unchanged on the 59 tasks shared with ASPIRE (50:8), so the task excluded by the sandbox does not drive it. 4.5. Where Do the Gains Come From? The matched subset concentrates on episodes where single policies fail (Figure 5). The full router solves 48/72 episodes and is the only method to outperform the best single policy (+11.1%, 𝑝=0.039 unadjusted); the gate contrast below is the one that survives Holm correction (adjusted 𝑝=0.014, against 0.12 for this gain). Both modules contribute. Without route memory the judge must find the better policy by trial and error (39/72, 𝑝=0.078). Replacing the judge gate by the exception gate costs 15.3% (12:1, 𝑝=0.003): of the twelve episodes only the full router solves, seven are failed first runs rescued by escalation and five are replay variance. The comparison is at matched escalation budget: REA-Ms cap 𝐾=1 never binds, because all three of its escalations ran to the 4,000-step horizon, so with 𝐾=2 it would behave identically on every episode. The subset is selected for Fix failures; on unselected seeds the same gate contrast is +3.1% (Section 4.4). Uncoordinated recovery 10 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control Table 2 Comparison with VLA and code policies on RoboTwin 2.0. Each row evaluates the same 50 clean and 50 randomized scenes. Success counts and overall rates are shown; best per column is bold. Historical baselines and the VLA extension were run in different windows; MEDex uses separate host. Protocols and policy budgets are detailed in Appendix C.1. Where should System 2 sit? Figure 6 moves the agent through every online role on one library and host. Asking it to pick the policies at dispatch and recovery (REA-A) changes success by +0.5% (6:3, 𝑝=0.51) while adding selection call. completion judge that reads scene captions, whether the agent or text model, costs 1.32.2% and spends 7.99.6 per episode in System 2 calls, since on this strong library the exception gate suffices; as direct Cartesian policy it solves none of 600 episodes, second failing interface after the one-token probe (Appendix C.4). The brain pays off offline and, where policies fail silently, as visual judge. Why can noisy judge help? Its final verdicts are barely more accurate than always answering done (0.72 vs. 0.67 matched) or less (0.67 vs. 0.75 LIBERO-Pro), but their done decisions are precise (0.83, 0.905), and re-running completed task usually keeps it completed: by the proxy attribution of Table 14, re-runs convert 24% (19%) of failed first runs and undo 5% (9%) of successful ones. Measured on final verdicts only, this is consistent explanation, not tested mechanism; the +15.3% of this subset is stress test, and +3.1% on unselected seeds (Section 4.4) is the estimate to expect. 4.6. VLA and Code Policies Share System 0 Learned policies run in the same embodied runtime. We evaluate REA on 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, with one clean and one randomized scene per task (100 episodes). REA (VLA policies) selects among seven VLA models; REA (VLA policies + Code policies) adds Python code policy to the same candidate pool. Both use learned System 1 selector that predicts success from the initial instruction, camera images and robot state, chooses the highest-scoring policy, and retains it for the episode. VLA policies execute native action chunks; the code policy generates and executes Cartesian gripper command at each decision. This directly instantiates both policy types as System 0 under the common runtime interface (Appendix C.1). Combining VLA and code policies improves success. Table 2 shows 84% success with VLA policies and 86% with the mixed pool, compared with 80% for the MEDex single-VLA baseline. Both routed VLA configurations solve 44/50 clean scenes. Adding code raises randomized successes from 40/50 to 42/50, with two additional successes and no lost VLA-only successes. These results provide direct evidence for VLA execution and episode-level dispatch across learned and programmatic policies under the same REA interface. Policy choices and training details are in Appendix C.1. 11 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control Figure 7 Results of portability experiments. Bars show success rates; whiskers indicate Wilson 95% confidence intervals. BEHAVIOR-1K: test instances 110 of five R1Pro pick-up tasks (50 episodes), 1,500 per episode, gpt-6-astra for every method; Codex + GPT-6 and ASPIRE are frozen programs (the ASPIRE-style Fix loop), Agents SDK and Show-Harness are online agents. RoboTwin 2.0: the two test sets (200 scenes, 50 tasks, half clean and half randomized), at most 40 decisions per episode. Unitree G1 of real walk-and-push-chair trials and AlohaMini2 of real block-placement trials are both manually reviewed. Show-Harness was not run on either real robot due to the low success rates. Details in Appendices C.2, D.1 and D.3. 4.7. Extensional Experiments on BEHAVIOR and RoboTwin-2 On BEHAVIOR-1K (R1Pro, Isaac Sim), which needed only new backend, REA solves 27 of 50 test episodes over five pick-up tasks, the most of the compared methods: 25 for the online Agents SDK agent with the same model, tools and budget, 18 each for the Codex and ASPIRE-style Fix programs, and 3 for Show-Harness (Figure 7, Table 15). Against the Agents SDK agent the margin is not significant (7:5, 𝑝=0.77) and comes from one task, camera (5 against 1); against the frozen-program baselines it is 13:4 (𝑝=0.049) and 12:3 (𝑝=0.035). In the separate 200-scene RoboTwin 2.0 transfer study, fast reflex model serves as the System 0 policy and the router hands single decisions to deliberate model. Run side by side with the Codex CLI on the 200 test scenes, REA solves 97 against 75 (42:20, 𝑝=0.007). Run again on later night it solves 133, against 105 for ASPIRE, 103 for the Agents SDK agent and 12 for Show-Harness (𝑝<0.001 each); the same configuration moved by 36 scenes between the two nights, so only the side-by-side pair compares methods without window effect (Appendix C.2). 4.8. Real Robot Experiments on Unitree-G1 On Unitree G1 humanoid that must walk to chair and push it, with the same model and System 0 policies for every method and success judged on site, REA succeeds in 8 of 10 trials, against 5 for the Agents SDK agent, 4 for Codex and 2 for ASPIRE (𝑝=0.023; Table 18). Figure 2 shows REA episodes on all three simulators and on the real robot, including LIBERO-Pro test episode in which the judge gate climbs the full escalation ladder. 12 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control (a) Agent methods (b) VLA + Code Codex Agents SDK ASPIRE REA 5/10 4/10 8/10 10/ 𝜋0.5 REA (𝜋0.5 + Code) 3/10 8/10 0 100 0 50 100 Success rate (%) Success rate (%) Figure 8 Experimetal results of AlohaMini2 block placement. Success rates in two separate studies, with ten trials per method; labels give successful trials. (a) Four agent methods. (b) 𝜋0.5 alone and REA routing between 𝜋0.5 and Code. The two studies retain their own protocols and timing measures (Appendices D.3 and D.4). 4.9. Real-World Block Placement on AlohaMini2 We evaluate the AlohaMini2 right arm on grasping an object outside box, releasing it inside, and leaving it stable after the gripper retracts. In 40-trial comparison with ten valid trials per method, REA completes 10/10 trials, compared with 8/10 for ASPIRE, 5/10 for Codex and 4/10 for Agents SDK (Figure 8). Each trial allows up to three grasp attempts without fixed total time limit, and outcomes use the original manual review (Appendix D.3). In separate 20-trial controller study, REA routes asynchronously between 𝜋0.5 and Code controller and succeeds in 8/10 trials, versus 3/10 for 𝜋0.5 alone. Placement failures fall from five to zero, while both groups have two grasp failures; Code executes in five of the ten REA trials. The groups were collected on different days with their original session settings (Appendix D.4). REA has higher observed success and longer mean recorded time in both studies: 1,618.0 versus 1,314.9 for ASPIRE in the four-method study, and 128.89 versus 16.57 of active time for 𝜋0.5 alone in the controller study (Tables 20 and 21). 5. Discussion Use the brain ahead of time or at policy returns, never inside running policy. Dispatching from route memory outperforms each individual policy-generation method and is as accurate as asking an agent at every dispatch, at no online cost (Table 1, Figure 6); consulted in the loop, the brain adds waiting (Figure 4); consulted only when policy returns, noisy judge adds success where policies fail silently, at extra time (Table 7, Figure 5). The brain still sets the ceiling (success rates differ by 2047% across methods), and the router decides how much of it is reached. The gate should be chosen per library on development episodes: the free exception gate suffices when policies rarely fail, the judge gate pays for its calls when they fail silently. One interface, different selectors. The shared Run interface supports both route-memory lookup and learned policy selection. In the RoboTwin 2.0 extension, learned selector chooses one of seven VLAs or Python policy from the initial observation and keeps that choice fixed throughout the episode (Section 4.6, Appendix C.1). This study evaluates the shared policy interface and initial selection; recovery-gate effects are evaluated separately on LIBERO-Pro. 13 REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control 6. Conclusion REA separates an embodied system into System 2 brain, an embodied router and fast System 0 policies under one aligned runtime. On 60 LIBERO-Pro tasks it beats each method that contributes policies to its pool and is the fastest timed pipeline without any online brain call. Its gains come from the router rather than larger pool: route memory dispatches as well as an online agent at no model cost, and the boundary-triggered judge helps where policies fail silently. The same interfaces carry over to BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboTwin 2.0 and real Unitree G1, where REA solves the most episodes. The separate 100-episode RoboTwin 2.0 study demonstrates VLA and code policies within the same runtime: REA reaches 84% with VLA policies and 86% with VLA+code, compared with 80% for MEDex, the strongest single VLA baseline. We hope REA becomes shared platform for developing and comparing embodied brains and fast policies. REA: Routed Embodied Agent Runtime for Asynchronous Brain-Cerebellum Control

The VLA study uses fixed set of 100 RoboTwin 2.0 scenes: 50 tasks, each with one clean and one randomized scene, taken from episode 0 of the scene manifest.
